One primary concept each, checked for duplicated required answers as well as duplicated labels. Q1 the species concept and what it cannot do · Q2 speciation end to end, once with a geographical barrier and once with a temporal one · Q3 the barriers themselves, prezygotic and postzygotic · Q4 classification against phylogeny, and the clause that separates them · Q5 five different ways of reading relatedness off a figure · Q6 the specimen's own alignment block · Q7 why molecular methods win and where they stop working · Q8 the three classification methods and their limitations, at essay length. Declared overlaps, and there are three. The advantages of molecular methods are stated in Q4(d) as a one-mark reason, argued in Q7(a) as a two-mark explain, and set against their limitations in Q8 at essay length; the three schemes score different things. Multiple sequence alignment appears in Q6(d) as the method you must explain performing and in Q7(b) as the phrase its scheme makes compulsory. Reproductive isolation appears in Q1 as the definition's test, in Q2 as the endpoint of speciation and in Q3 as the barriers themselves; no two of those schemes accept the same answer.

Nothing from Cluster 1 or Cluster 2, and nothing from Books 8 or 9. Variation, natural selection, the three modes, homology as evidence, the fossil record, drift, gene flow, heterozygote advantage and Hardy-Weinberg are all tested in the first two drills and none of them is required here. Out of scope under 9477 and therefore absent: polyploidy, the four non-biological species concepts, binomial nomenclature and Linnaeus, cladistics vocabulary, adaptive radiation and mass extinction, and the distance-matrix formalism. All of them are not in the learning outcomes.

Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Q5 Q6 Q7 Q8

Question 1 [6 marks]

(a) Figure 1.1 shows aligned mitochondrial DNA sequences for a modern human, a Neanderthal, a chimpanzee, an orangutan, a gorilla and a macaque. Explain why orangutans and gorillas are considered to be different biological species. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain why orangutans and gorillas are considered to be different biological species. [2]

1. [INFERRED: no official key; the specimen papers ship without one.]

2. Under the biological species concept, a species is a group of organisms of similar morphology and physiology that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

3. Orangutans and gorillas do not interbreed in the wild and could not produce fertile offspring if they did, so they are reproductively isolated.

4. There is no gene flow between them and their gene pools remain separate. This is reflected in the differences in their DNA base sequences.

5. Wording note. The school's own definition is a population or group of populations whose members have the potential to interbreed in nature and produce viable, fertile offspring, and which cannot produce viable, fertile offspring with members of other populations. Three words do work. In nature rules out hybrids that occur only in captivity. Viable rules out a zygote that dies early. Fertile rules out the mule. Giving fertile alone misses hybrid inviability; giving viable alone misses hybrid sterility.

(b) The biological species concept is one of the species concepts used to define a species. State two limitations of the biological species concept. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) State two limitations of the biological species concept. [2]

1. Cannot be applied to fossils.

2. Cannot be applied to asexual organisms as they do not interbreed.

3. There can still be gene flow between species that are morphologically distinct.

4. There can still be gene flow between species that are ecologically distinct.

5. The outcome's own count. LO 4(h) says explain the biological concept of the species and its limitations, so limitations are half the outcome, and the school lists four: fossils cannot be tested for reproductive isolation; the concept does not apply to organisms that reproduce asexually all or most of the time, including prokaryotes and self-fertilising species; species are designated by the absence of gene flow yet many morphologically and ecologically distinct species still exchange genes; and some individuals of the same species rarely interbreed, as with geographically separated populations of the same grass frog species.

(c) Bombus pratorum and Bombus terrestris are two British species of bumble bee. Describe how it is possible to confirm, over a longer period of time, whether B. pratorum and B. terrestris belong to different species. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Describe how it is possible to confirm, over a longer period of time, whether B. pratorum and B. terrestris belong to different species. [2]

1. Interbreed both species B. pratorum and B. terrestris.

2. If offspring are viable and fertile, they are considered as the same species.

3. If offspring are infertile, then they are considered as different species.

4. According to the biological species concept.

Question 2 [10 marks]

(a) Over thousands and millions of years, the Earth's climate is subject to natural periods of warming and cooling. Figure 8.1 is a diagram representing two mountains in the tropics during a warm phase and a cool phase in the Earth's climate. The shape of the lines corresponds to a vertical section through the mountains to show their height and shape. The distribution of rain forest vegetation with altitude is shown by the hatched shading.

Suggest how repeated changes in climate between the warm phase and cool phase shown in Figure 8.1 may lead to the evolution of new species and greater species diversity. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Suggest how repeated changes in climate between the warm phase and cool phase may lead to the evolution of new species and greater species diversity. [5]

1. [INFERRED: no official key; the specimen papers ship without one.]

2. In the cool phase the rain forest extends to low altitude and the forest on the two mountains is joined into one continuous habitat, so the organisms form one population with gene flow between them.

3. In the warm phase the forest is restricted to the tops of the mountains, so the populations are separated into isolated patches with unsuitable, hotter lowland between them. They are geographically isolated, interbreeding stops, and there is no gene flow between them.

4. Different mutations arise at random in each isolated population, and because the environmental conditions and selection pressures on each mountain are slightly different, natural selection favours different alleles in each population. Genetic drift also acts, because the isolated populations are small.

5. Over many generations the allele frequencies of the two gene pools diverge, and the populations become increasingly different genetically and phenotypically.

6. Eventually the differences are so great that even when the cool phase brings the forests back together the two populations can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring. They are reproductively isolated and are therefore separate species. This is allopatric speciation.

7. Because the cycle of warm and cool phases is repeated many times, the process happens over and over and in many separate mountain groups, so more and more new species accumulate in the same region and species diversity increases.

8. Why this part matters more than its five marks. It is the highest-mark undifferentiated Book 7 part on the whole specimen, with no (i) and (ii) to supply the structure, and the command word is Suggest, not Explain, so there is no recall answer. The word geographical never appears in the stem; you have to see that a mountaintop forest patch is a geographical isolate. It maps almost exactly onto the school's four-stage model.

9. The four-stage model it maps onto. (1) A single population shares one gene pool and interbreeds freely. (2) A barrier develops and gene flow between the separated populations is interrupted. (3) The populations differentiate under different selection pressures and genetic drift, and reproductive isolating mechanisms begin to develop. (4) The barrier disappears and reproductive isolation is tested. If the populations are now unable to produce fertile, viable offspring, speciation is complete; if they still interbreed successfully, the process halts and a single species remains.

(b) B. pratorum and B. terrestris both live in Britain. They can often be found in the same location, as their geographical distributions overlap. Name the process by which these species of bees are formed. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Name the process by which these species of bees are formed. [1]

1. Sympatric speciation.

(c) Fig. 9.1 shows the number of worker bees of B. pratorum and B. terrestris observed at one location over a year. Using Fig. 9.1, and the information given, explain how an ancestral species might have evolved into the two species, B. pratorum and B. terrestris. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Using Fig. 9.1, explain how an ancestral species might have evolved into the two species. [4]

1. Random mutations give rise to different genetic variation within the ancestral population.

2. Selection pressure present in the overlapped geographical location.

3. Individuals with favourable phenotypes, or which have a selective advantage, will be selected for.

4. They have a higher probability of surviving and reproducing fertile and viable offspring.

5. They pass down favourable alleles to offspring, increasing the frequency of favourable alleles in the population.

6. Presence of a reproductive barrier, different breeding season.

7. Quoted from the figure: different breeding seasons, with B. pratorum worker numbers peaking in June and B. terrestris peaking in July.

8. No interbreeding between individuals in the populations, gene flow is disrupted, resulting in the emergence of different species.

Sources & concepts

Source: 9477 Specimen Paper 2 Q8(a), stem and Figure 8.1 verbatim (a); the key is [INFERRED], and points 8 and 9 are this build's notes from the specimen audit and the school's chapter 7.4 pp.80 to 82. TJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q9(b)(i), stem and key verbatim (b), with the overlapping-distribution sentence carried in from the paper's own Q9(b) preamble. TJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q9(b)(ii), stem, Fig. 9.1 and all eight marking points verbatim (c). Archetype: mechanism explain-chain run end to end, twice, on two different barrier types. This is the full-cycle question of this drill: part (a) runs allopatric speciation from one population through a geographical barrier to a tested reproductive isolation and back again, and part (c) runs the same model with the barrier supplied by timing rather than geography. Trap: stopping at geographic separation. The four-stage model exists because separation alone is Stage 2 of 4, and chapter 7.4 p.81 is explicit that if the reunited populations still interbreed successfully the process of speciation halts and a single species remains. An answer that ends at "the populations are separated and adapt differently" has described divergence, not speciation. In (c), the second trap is answering sympatric speciation with polyploidy: LO 4(j) names behavioural or physiological isolation within the same geographical location, and polyploid is not in the learning outcomes, so the answer comes from the barrier tables, not from chromosome doubling. The third trap in (c) is not quoting the figure; the scheme has a marking point for the two peak months. LOs: 4(j) throughout, both halves of it, geographical isolation (allopatric speciation) in (a) and behavioural or physiological isolation within the same geographical location (sympatric speciation) in (b) and (c). 4(d) in (a) point 4, genetic drift in small isolated populations. Concepts fused:** (1) reading a habitat as continuous or fragmented off an altitude profile; (2) a physical barrier blocking gene flow; (3) independent mutation in each isolate; (4) different selection pressures driving divergence; (5) drift accelerating divergence in small isolates; (6) the reunion as the test of reproductive isolation; (7) repetition of the cycle generating diversity, not just one species; (8) temporal isolation as a barrier that needs no geography; (9) quoting two peak months as the evidence for it; (10) the structural difference between the two modes, which is when the reproductive barrier appears.

Question 3 [8 marks]

(a) It was shown that different species of the cat family no longer interbreed. Suggest and explain two reasons why interbreeding was not possible. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Suggest and explain two reasons why interbreeding was not possible between different cat species. [3]

1. Compulsory point. Different species within the cat family have accumulated genetic differences due to various factors such as mutation, natural selection, and genetic drift.

2. Then any two of the following. Differing geographical location or barrier leading to no opportunity for interaction.

3. The species have specific mating behaviours and courtship rituals that are essential for successful reproduction, and these behaviours differ significantly between species.

4. Physical differences in reproductive organs can prevent successful mating between different species.

5. Temporal isolation occurs when different species have different mating seasons or times.

6. These genetic differences can lead to incompatibility between the DNA of different species, making it impossible for their gametes to successfully combine and create viable embryos.

(b) Mimulus lewisii and Mimulus cardinalis can breed together in the laboratory to produce F1 hybrids. The F1 hybrids produce 50% fewer seeds than either of the two parent species. Explain how the reduced production of seeds by the inter-species F1 hybrids can act as a post-zygotic isolating mechanism. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain how the reduced production of seeds by the F1 hybrids can act as a post-zygotic isolating mechanism. [3]

1. Any three. F1 hybrids have fewer F2 offspring / reduced reproductive fitness. Reject fewer seeds without further elaboration.

2. Hence they are outcompeted by the parent species.

3. Parent species or phenotypes are better adapted or more successful. Accept that the F1 hybrid has a selective disadvantage and is selected against, but only if reference is made to the parents.

4. Reference to disruptive selection.

5. Hybrid breakdown / hybrid line not sustained long-term. Reject explanations pertaining to extinction.

(c) The collared flycatcher, Ficedula albicollis, and the pied flycatcher, F. hypoleuca, are two closely related species of bird whose breeding areas overlap on the island of Oland, Sweden, where small numbers of hybrid flycatchers are produced. Table 10.1 shows the percentage of males of each bird type with normal sperm: F. albicollis 68, F. hypoleuca 78, male hybrid 0. Analysis showed that all female hybrids were sterile. Table 10.2 shows, for each male-female pair of a nest, the percentage of clutches with eggs that hatched and the percentage of extra-pair nestlings: F. albicollis male with F. albicollis female, 94.5% and 17.2%; F. hypoleuca male with F. hypoleuca female, 89.3% and 22.4%; hybrid male with F. albicollis or F. hypoleuca female, 38.0% and 100.0%. Using the data from Table 10.1 and Table 10.2, explain why hybrid males do not pass on their genes to their nestlings. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Using Table 10.1 and Table 10.2, explain why hybrid males do not pass on their genes to their nestlings. [2]

1. As 0% of hybrid males produce normal sperm, hybrid males are not able to fertilise any eggs, despite forming pairs with F. albicollis or F. hypoleuca females.

2. In pairs with hybrid males, all offspring, 100%, are fathered by other males, that is, all nests with a hybrid male in the male-female pair were parented by another male of the same species as the female.

Sources & concepts

Source: CJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q9(c), stem and key verbatim including the compulsory first point (a), with "different species of the cat family" carried in from the paper's own Q9 preamble. School (HCI) Prelim 2023 P2 Q8(b)(ii), stem and key verbatim including both reject lines (b), with the two Mimulus species and the laboratory cross carried in from the paper's own Q8(b)(i) preamble. TMJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q10(b), stem and key verbatim (c), with Table 10.1 and Table 10.2 written into the stem as their own values. Archetype: mechanism explain-chain feeding a data reading. Part (c) is the shape the papers sets most often for this outcome: a table of percentages, and the mark is for tying the right figure to the right claim. Trap: naming a barrier without saying what it does. The scheme in (a) requires the compulsory genetic-divergence point first, so a list of four barrier names with no cause scores at most two. In (b), saying "the hybrids make fewer seeds" and stopping, which the scheme rejects by name, because the isolating effect is that the hybrid line is not sustained and is outcompeted by the parents. The wider trap is losing the prezygotic and postzygotic split: prezygotic barriers prevent formation of zygotes by blocking fertilisation, postzygotic barriers act after fertilisation and prevent the hybrid zygote developing into a viable, fertile adult. Habitat, temporal, behavioural, mechanical and gametic isolation are prezygotic; hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility and hybrid breakdown are postzygotic. LOs: 4(j) throughout, the isolating mechanisms by which new species are formed and kept apart. 4(h) in (c), since hybrid sterility is what the biological species concept's word fertile is guarding against. Concepts fused: (1) accumulated genetic divergence as the precondition for any barrier; (2) habitat isolation; (3) behavioural isolation through courtship; (4) mechanical isolation through reproductive structures; (5) temporal isolation through mating season; (6) gametic incompatibility; (7) reduced hybrid fitness as a postzygotic barrier; (8) hybrid breakdown against hybrid sterility; (9) reading a sperm-normality percentage as a fertility statement; (10) extra-pair paternity as the evidence that the hybrid male fathered nothing.

Question 4 [6 marks]

(a) Living organisms display an incredible diversity in shape and function. To understand this diversity, biologists use classification systems and phylogeny. Explain the relationship between classification and phylogeny. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain the relationship between classification and phylogeny. [2]

1. Classification is the organisation of species into groups based on shared characteristics, and it uses a naming system.

2. Classification may not take into consideration the evolutionary relationship between the species.

3. Phylogeny is the organisation of species according to particular characteristics, mainly molecular homology, which takes into consideration the evolutionary relationship between the species, and each organism is assigned a position on the phylogenetic tree.

4. Examiner's comment: correct points required in the explanation are mirrored in the syllabus.

(b) Table 10.1 shows the taxonomic classification information of the kakapos. Describe the principles which scientists use to classify organisms into taxonomic groups. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Describe the principles which scientists use to classify organisms into taxonomic groups. [2]

1. Compulsory marking point. Scientists nest or place smaller groups within bigger groups in a hierarchical manner.

2. The grouping is based on morphological, anatomical or physiological similarities.

(c) State two pieces of evidence that can be used in determining the phylogenetic history of a species. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) State two pieces of evidence that can be used in determining the phylogenetic history of a species. [1]

1. The phylogenetic history of a species can be obtained by comparing homologous morphological structures and homologous molecular sequences with those of other organisms.

(d) Five species of Pacific salmon were grouped twice, once as classification X, based on morphological characteristics, and once as classification Y, based on genetic characteristics. State one reason why classification Y is a better representation of evolutionary relationships than classification X. [1]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) State one reason why the genetic classification is a better representation of evolutionary relationships than the morphological one. [1]

1. Molecular methods can be used for all organisms, living or dead. All living organisms have nucleic acids and proteins so comparisons can be made, and molecular methods can also be applied to dead or extinct organisms as long as DNA or protein can be obtained, for example DNA extracted from fossils.

2. Or, molecular methods are objective. DNA sequences in the form of A, T, C and G are unambiguous, so differences between organisms can be determined objectively, unlike comparing morphological structures such as shape, which are hard to distinguish and give subjective interpretations.

3. Or, molecular methods are quantitative. Molecular data can be converted to numerical form for computation and analysis, so the degree of relatedness can be inferred by calculating the number of nucleotide or amino acid differences, and the data can be uploaded to online databases for retrieval anywhere, which is not possible for a morphological method that requires physical specimens.

4. Or, molecular methods are more accurate in establishing evolutionary relationships. They avoid the pitfalls of convergent evolution, where organisms appear morphologically similar because of adaptation to similar habitats but do not share a common ancestor, for example the flying squirrel and the sugar glider, and conversely they can establish the relationship between organisms that look very different but are closely related, because major phenotypic differences may rest on small genetic differences.

Sources & concepts

Source: ASRJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q9(a), stem, key and examiner comment verbatim (a). SAJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q10(d), stem and key verbatim including the compulsory hierarchical-nesting point (b). EJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q2(a)(iii), stem and key verbatim (c). TJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q9(a)(ii), stem and the whole four-way key verbatim (d), with the two classifications described in the stem from the paper's own Q9(a)(i) preamble. Archetype: recall and define, which the papers sets rarely for this Book but which LO 4(i) and LO 4(k) ask for directly. The definitions are printed almost word for word in the syllabus, which is why the ASRJC examiner comment says so. Trap: treating classification and phylogeny as the same thing because both group organisms. The clause that separates them is that classification groups by shared characteristics and may not consider evolutionary relationship, while phylogeny does. LO 4(i) and LO 4(k) are separate outcomes for exactly this reason. The scope trap sits next to it: binomial, Linnaeus, taxonomy, taxa, genus and kingdom all are not in the learning outcomes, so learn the eight ranks once as vocabulary for reading a question and stop. The principle that is examinable is the hierarchical nesting, which is (b)'s compulsory point. LOs: 4(i) in (a), (b), (c) and (d), defining biological classification and describing how evolutionary relationship is established. 4(k) in (a), defining phylogeny. 4(l) in (d), the advantages of molecular methods. Concepts fused:** (1) classification defined by shared characteristics; (2) the clause that it may ignore evolutionary relationship; (3) phylogeny defined by evolutionary relationship; (4) hierarchical nesting as the organising principle; (5) morphological and molecular homology as the two evidence types; (6) universality of molecular data; (7) objectivity of a sequence against subjectivity of a shape; (8) quantifiability and databases; (9) convergent evolution as the failure mode of a morphological classification.

Question 5 [9 marks]

(a) The flow diagram shows an investigation into the blood proteins of four species, W, X, Y and Z. Foreign blood proteins cause the production of antibodies. Mixing an antibody with its corresponding protein causes a precipitate. The four species, in alphabetical order, were chicken, chimpanzee, human and mouse. Which row correctly identifies the species involved? [1]

species Wspecies Xspecies Yspecies Z
Achickenchimpanzeemousehuman
Bmousechimpanzeechickenhuman
Chumanmousechimpanzeechicken
Dchickenmousechimpanzeehuman
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which row correctly identifies the species involved? [1]

1. D. [INFERRED: no official key; the specimen papers ship without one.]

2. The chicken antibodies were raised against human serum proteins, so the more similar a species' proteins are to human proteins, the more antibody binds and the more precipitate forms.

3. Species Z gives 100% precipitate, so it must be human itself, because the proteins are identical.

4. Species Y at 64% is the chimpanzee, the most closely related of the remaining species and therefore the one sharing the most similar amino acid sequences.

5. Species X at 29% is the mouse, a mammal but far more distantly related.

6. Species W gives 0%, so it is the chicken. The chicken's immune system recognises its own proteins as self and makes no antibodies against them, so no precipitate can form. Percentage precipitate therefore falls as evolutionary distance from humans increases.

7. Why this question is hard. It is not a tree question and it is not about DNA. It is immunological distance, which the school's notes never teach. The transferable skill is the accumulation argument from chapter 7.2 p.24: more similarity means closer relationship. A candidate who has only memorised "compare DNA sequences" cannot do it.

(b) Prion protein is found on the surface of neurons in vertebrates. The gene coding for this protein has been sequenced in 33 species of vertebrates. The differences in base sequence have been used to construct a phylogeny for these 33 vertebrates. The phylogeny is shown in the diagram below. Which row correctly deduces the evolutionary relationships stated according to the base sequence of the prion gene? [1]

the species most similar to that of Homo sapiensthe species most different from that of Homo sapiens
APan troglodytesGallus gallus
BPongo pygmaeusBos taurus
CGorilla gorillaMacaca fuscata
DGorilla gorillaGallus gallus
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Which row correctly deduces the evolutionary relationships according to the base sequence of the prion gene? [1]

1. The key is D. [INFERRED: no official key beyond the answer letter.] 71.03% of the cohort answered correctly.

2. On this tree Gorilla gorilla is the immediate sister branch to Homo sapiens, so it is the most similar.

3. Gallus gallus branches off earliest, closest to the root, so it is the most different.

4. A fails on the first column: on this particular tree Pan troglodytes is not the immediate sister branch, even though a different dataset might place it there. Read the tree in front of you, not the phylogeny you remember.

5. B fails on both columns: Pongo pygmaeus branches deeper than the gorilla, and Bos taurus sits inside the mammal clade, so it is far closer to Homo sapiens than the bird is.

6. C fails on the second column: Macaca fuscata is an Old World monkey and therefore inside the primate clade, whereas Gallus gallus is outside the mammals altogether.

(c) Fig. 1.4 shows a phylogenetic tree of different bacteria species A, B, C, D and E. The root is node I. From I one branch leads to species E and the other leads to node H. From node H one branch leads to node F, which splits into species A and species B; the other branch from H leads to node G, which splits into species C and species D. Discuss two evolutionary conclusions which can be made about the relationships between the different bacteria species. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Discuss two evolutionary conclusions which can be made about the relationships between the bacteria species. [2]

1. Any two. Species A, B, C and D share more common characteristics with each other than any of them share with species E, and species I is the common ancestor of A, B, C, D and E.

2. Species H is the most recent common ancestor for A and D.

3. Species F is a common ancestor for A and B.

4. Species G is a common ancestor for C and D.

5. Reject any reference to taxonomy terms, for example same genus.

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Draw a phylogenetic tree to include the western grey kangaroo, showing only the smallest clade which comprises all kangaroo species. [2]

1. Correct drawing of the revised phylogenetic tree that includes the western grey kangaroo with the correct time point of divergence shown, 1.5 million years ago.

2. Correct inclusion of labels: swamp wallaby, common wallaroo, black wallaroo, red kangaroo, western grey kangaroo, eastern grey kangaroo.

(e) Fig. 9.2 is a phylogenetic tree showing how the two species and other species of bumble bees evolve from a distant common ancestor, with the 2 species of interest boxed up. The DNA sequences of the mitochondrial genomes were analysed to provide molecular data. With reference to Fig. 9.2, explain why there is insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the evolutionary relationships between the two species of bumble bees. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (e)

(e) Explain why there is insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the evolutionary relationships between the two species of bumble bees. [3]

1. The phylogenetic tree was constructed based on only molecular homology to determine how the two species recently diverged from their common ancestors, or it was constructed using mitochondrial genomes alone, which is not representative of entire genomes.

2. They may still be able to interbreed or mate to produce viable and fertile offspring.

3. Additional data based on various species concepts, such as morphological or ecological, are required before they can be classified as two separate species.

Archetype: phylogenetic tree and relatedness reading. This archetype has no analogue anywhere else in the syllabus, and it is where this Book's marks concentrate. It is also the one figure archetype worth drilling as pure reading rather than as stimulus for an explain. Trap: the three stock tree misreadings, all corrected on chapter 7.5 pp.112 to 113. First, a tree does not show absolute age: branching order tells you which common ancestor is more recent, and nothing about when a species evolved, unless the branch lengths are declared proportional to time. Second, a taxon does not evolve from the taxon next to it; two neighbouring tips both descend from the common ancestor at their shared node. Third, any node can be rotated without changing the tree, so the same phylogeny redrawn with two branches swapped is the standard distractor. In (a) the extra trap is inverting the scale: the highest precipitate is the species the antibodies were raised against, and the zero is the animal that made them. LOs: 4(k) throughout, phylogeny as the organisation of species to show evolutionary relationships. 4(i) in (c) and (d), how evolutionary relationship is established. 4(l) in (a) and (e), reconstructing relationships from molecular data and the limits of doing so. 4(h) in (e) point 2, since the tree alone cannot settle whether two lineages are separate species. Concepts fused: (1) protein similarity read off a precipitate percentage; (2) self-recognition explaining the zero; (3) sister-group relationships read off a radial tree; (4) the deepest branch as the most distant taxon; (5) root, node and tip as vocabulary for stating a conclusion; (6) most recent common ancestor found by tracing back to convergence; (7) drawing a divergence onto an existing tree at a stated date; (8) a clade defined as the smallest group containing all named members; (9) one gene or one genome as an inadequate sample; (10) a tree as a hypothesis that other species concepts have to corroborate.

Question 6 [10 marks]

The calculation that Mitochondrial Eve lived between 150 000 and 200 000 years ago is based on the idea of a mean rate of mutation of DNA. Mitochondrial DNA has a higher mutation rate than chromosomal DNA, and mtDNA is passed to offspring only from the mother.

(a) Suggest one reason why a higher mutation rate is useful for this type of study. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Suggest one reason why a higher mutation rate is useful for this type of study. [1]

1. [INFERRED: no official key; the specimen papers ship without one.]

2. A higher mutation rate means more base differences accumulate in a given period of time, so there is enough variation to detect and compare even over the short timescale of modern human evolution.

3. This gives greater resolution when distinguishing between closely related individuals or populations, and a more precise estimate of when they diverged.

4. The general rule behind it. DNA coding for ribosomal RNA changes relatively slowly, so it resolves taxa that diverged hundreds of millions of years ago. Mitochondrial DNA evolves relatively rapidly, so it resolves recent evolutionary events. Match the molecule to the timescale.

(b) Suggest one reason why maternal inheritance of mtDNA is useful for this type of study. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Suggest one reason why maternal inheritance of mtDNA is useful for this type of study. [1]

1. [INFERRED] Because mtDNA is inherited only down the female line and is not mixed with any paternal DNA, it is passed on unchanged apart from mutations, so all the differences between individuals must be due to mutation alone.

2. This means a single unbroken maternal lineage can be traced backwards to one common female ancestor.

(c) Figure 1.1 shows the nucleotide base sequence of a short fragment of DNA from a modern human and the corresponding base sequences from a Neanderthal and four other primate species. Chimpanzee, orangutan and gorilla are species of ape, while the macaque is a type of monkey. Complete the list in Table 1.1 to place the primates from Figure 1.1 in order of the closeness of their evolutionary relationship to humans. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Place the primates in order of the closeness of their evolutionary relationship to humans. [1]

1. [INFERRED] Working down from the top box, which already contains modern human: Neanderthal, chimpanzee, gorilla, orangutan, macaque.

2. Number of base differences from the modern human sequence: Neanderthal 0, chimpanzee 2, gorilla 4, orangutan 5, macaque 10.

(d) Explain how you used the information in Figure 1.1 to work out your answer to (c). [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Explain how you used the information in Figure 1.1 to work out your answer. [2]

1. [INFERRED] I compared each species' sequence with the modern human sequence base by base and counted the number of positions at which the bases differ, giving Neanderthal 0, chimpanzee 2, gorilla 4, orangutan 5 and macaque 10 differences.

2. I then placed the species in order of increasing number of differences.

3. This works because base differences accumulate as mutations at a roughly constant rate over time, so the fewer the differences between two species, the more recently they shared a common ancestor and the more closely related they are.

4. What this part is really testing. It asks you to explain your own method, not to state the answer, and it is worth twice as many marks as the answer itself. Saying two sequences look similar, with no count, does not demonstrate the method. LO 4(l) names multiple sequence alignment (nucleotide and amino acid) outright, and the same counting runs on amino acid substitutions in a protein alignment.

5. Why the alignment has to come first. Closely related species probably differ at only one or a few sites, so alignment is easy. Distantly related species have different bases at many sites and may have different lengths, because insertions and deletions accumulate over long periods, and those may not align cleanly, making comparison very difficult. An indel shifts everything downstream, so sequences must be realigned before differences are counted.

(e) In 1997, Krings and his co-workers analysed the mtDNA of 994 diverse modern humans, one Neanderthal fossil and nine chimpanzees, and compared each of these 1004 samples with each of the 994 modern human sequences, recording the number of nucleotide differences for each pairwise comparison. These differences in mtDNA have little or no effect on mitochondrial function. Each type of comparison in Figure 1.2 shows the same pattern of genetic variation. Name this pattern of genetic variation. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (e)

(e) Name the pattern of genetic variation shown by all three distributions. [1]

1. [INFERRED] Continuous variation, that is, a normal distribution.

(f) Describe and explain the results shown in Figure 1.2. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (f)

(f) Describe and explain the results shown in Figure 1.2. [4]

1. [INFERRED] All three sets of comparisons give a bell-shaped, normally distributed curve showing continuous variation, because the number of differences is the sum of many independently accumulated mutations.

2. The modern human against modern human comparisons have the fewest differences, peaking at about 7 to 8 and ranging from 0 to about 17, because all modern humans share a very recent common ancestor, so relatively few mutations have had time to accumulate since they diverged.

3. The modern human against Neanderthal comparisons peak higher, at about 25 to 26 differences, because modern humans and Neanderthals diverged from a common ancestor much longer ago, so more mutations have accumulated in each lineage.

4. The modern human against chimpanzee comparisons peak highest of all, at about 55 differences, because the human and chimpanzee lineages separated longest ago of the three. The number of differences is therefore proportional to the time since the two lineages last shared a common ancestor.

5. Because the three distributions do not overlap at all, the Neanderthal falls completely outside the range of variation found within modern humans, which is evidence that Neanderthals were a separate group and not simply an extreme variant of modern humans.

6. Marking convention. This is a describe and explain for four marks, which is two describe marks requiring quoted values and two explain marks. Schemes in this Book carry instructions of the form relevant supporting data must be quoted.

This is Book 7's single largest presence on the official specimen, and (c) and (d) together are three marks for counting differences and ranking by count. If one thing in this Book is drilled to fluency, it is this. Trap: counting similarities instead of differences. The scoring version counts base differences from the reference sequence and ranks by count, on the principle that more differences means longer since divergence. The second trap is the premise: converting a difference count into a divergence time assumes that the rate of accumulation of mutations has remained relatively constant over time, which is the assumption any "suggest a limitation" question attacks. The third is failing to quote values in (f), which costs two of the four marks. Reach-back to Book 2 in (e), since the pattern named is continuous variation. Concepts fused: (1) mutation rate matched to the timescale of the question; (2) rRNA against mtDNA; (3) uniparental inheritance removing recombination as a confounder; (4) tracing a single maternal lineage; (5) counting base differences in an alignment; (6) ranking by count; (7) explaining your own method as a metacognitive ask; (8) why indels break an alignment; (9) the molecular clock assumption; (10) reading three non-overlapping distributions; (11) quoting peak values as describe marks; (12) using non-overlap to argue that Neanderthals were a separate group.

Question 7 [9 marks]

(a) Explain two advantages of using molecular methods in classifying organisms compared to using similarities in morphology. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain two advantages of using molecular methods in classifying organisms compared to using similarities in morphology. [2]

1. Any two. Molecular data are quantifiable and open to statistical analysis, whereas there is limited morphological data available.

2. Molecular data are unambiguous and objective, whereas morphological data may differ depending on the way in which it was classified.

3. Molecular methods are not affected by convergent evolution, whereas some characteristics may be analogous, so similar morphology may not have been inherited from a common ancestor.

4. Molecular methods allow a wider range of organisms to be analysed based on a common gene or amino acid sequence, against limited options for morphology based on shared characteristics.

5. The alternative wording from the same school's reprint of this question. Molecular data such as nucleotide and amino acid sequences are quantifiable, in abundance and open to statistical analysis. Protein and nucleic acid sequence data are precise and accurate, which facilitates the objective assessment of evolutionary relationships. Molecular data is based strictly on heritable material. All organisms can be compared with the use of some molecular data, as all living organisms have nucleic acids and proteins.

(b) Fig. 9.3 shows the evolutionary relationships between three species of American spadefoot toad. Explain how analysis of DNA allowed the evolutionary relationships shown in Fig. 9.3 to be determined. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain how analysis of DNA allowed the evolutionary relationships shown in Fig. 9.3 to be determined. [3]

1. Correctly quoted data, for example that S. hammondii and S. bombifrons have the fewest genetic differences, or are the most genetically similar.

2. Reference to multiple sequence alignment. MP2 is required for full marks.

3. Reference to counting nucleotide differences or similarities.

4. Interprets that fewer nucleotide differences means more closely related, and less time since divergence or less time to the common ancestor, or the reverse argument.

5. Ignore molecular clock; a phylogeny shows evolutionary relationships, whereas a molecular clock estimates when lineages diverged.

6. Use of bioinformatic tools, a database, software or BLAST.

7. Examiner's note. The divergence time was already provided in the figure, so there was no need to explain how it was derived. The focus of the question was on constructing phylogeny directly from sequence data: aligning sequences, comparing nucleotide differences, and applying bioinformatics tools.

(c) Conclusions about evolutionary relationships between modern humans and Neanderthals were drawn from a comparison of short nucleotide sequences from one individual of each species. Explain why any such conclusions need to be treated with caution. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain why any such conclusions need to be treated with caution. [2]

1. The nucleotide sequences are only a small fraction of the whole genome, accept only studying part of one gene, and hence not representative of the entire genome.

2. There will be variation within each species due to mutations.

3. These sequences come from one individual from each species.

4. Any other valid point, for example insufficient morphological, physiological or anatomical data made available to make a conclusion.

5. Convergent evolution is rejected.

6. The outcome's own stated limitation. Findings are often inconclusive where several taxa diverged at nearly the same time in the distant past, because the differences may be apparent but not the order of their appearance.

(d) Other than the four DNA regions that were used in this study, a high proportion of non-coding DNA sequences are often used for further evolutionary studies. Suggest why it would be more advantageous to use the non-coding DNA to construct phylogenetic relationships. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Suggest why it would be more advantageous to use non-coding DNA to construct phylogenetic relationships. [2]

1. Higher mutation rates: non-coding regions often have higher mutation rates compared to coding regions, which can provide more variation to distinguish between closely related species or populations.

2. Non-coding DNA is not expressed, so the variation is neutral. Mutations in non-coding DNA may not affect gene expression and may not confer a selective advantage or disadvantage, so they are less likely to be eliminated by natural selection, preserving more evolutionary changes that can be informative for phylogenetic analysis.

3. Non-coding regions make up a large portion of the genome, so using these regions allows for a more comprehensive representation of genetic variation across the genome, providing a more complete picture of evolutionary relationships.

Question 8 [15 marks]

Section B free-response essay. There are many methods to classify organisms. Describe some methods and explain their limitations. [15]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer

There are many methods to classify organisms. Describe some methods and explain their limitations. [15]

1. Method 1, comparing morphological features. Several morphological features can be visually compared between organisms.

2. Organisms with similar structures are classified within the same group.

3. For example, animals which are warm-blooded and produce milk are classified as mammals, while animals which are cold-blooded, have dry skin covered with scales, and lay eggs are classified as reptiles, or any relevant example of grouping animals according to characteristics.

4. Organisms can be classified in a hierarchical manner, where they are first grouped based on a certain morphological trait, and further grouped based on another morphological trait, with reference to Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species, any three in the correct order.

5. Similar structures are likely to be inherited from a common ancestor, and on a phylogenetic tree or cladogram, those with similar structures will be classified in the same clade.

6. Limitations of method 1. It is not possible to classify organisms that had been extinct with no complete fossil records.

7. Some might have limited features for morphological comparisons, for example bacteria.

8. Comparison of morphological features is highly subjective and prone to errors.

9. Structures that look similar might not necessarily be inherited from a common ancestor; analogous structures might be mistaken for homologous structures, since similar traits could indicate organisms adapting in a similar manner under similar selection pressures.

10. For example, organisms with wings might be thought to have all inherited them from a common ancestor, but birds and insects that fly developed from different lineages, and placental and marsupial mammals look very similar and might be mistaken for the same species, but have in fact evolved from different ancestors.

11. Conversely, structures might look too different to be considered homologous, for example a whale's flippers and a bat's wings.

12. Evolutionary relationships of organisms classified under the same clade may not be identified based on morphological traits, that is, it is not possible to tell which organism within the same clade is more closely related to another by merely comparing morphological traits, for example humans, chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans are all primates but it is difficult to classify further which is more closely related by morphology alone.

13. Method 2, comparing molecular features. DNA, RNA or polypeptide sequences of organisms can be aligned and compared. Reference to chromosome painting, to DNA-DNA hybridisation, or to comparison of DNA banding patterns from gel electrophoresis or Southern blot.

14. The amount of differences can be quantified and is quantifiable.

15. The more differences in sequence, the more distantly related the organisms are, hence they are classified under different clades evolved from different common ancestors in a phylogenetic tree.

16. Certain bases or amino acids might be conserved at certain positions; these are likely to indicate common ancestry and place the organisms in the same group.

17. Limitations of method 2. It is difficult to classify organisms with no fossil records, or with fossil records so poorly preserved that DNA cannot be extracted.

18. Current technology only allows the comparison of short sequences; whole genome comparison is still not available, so the classification might be based on one or a few genes only, which might not be accurate.

19. Method 3, comparing biogeography. The geographic distribution of organisms over a period of time can suggest evolutionary relationship, based on the principle that each species originated only once.

20. Similar morphological or molecular features observed between organisms can only be classified under the same group or lineage if they existed in the same geographical location in the course of evolution. For example, placental and marsupial mammals exist on different continents, suggesting that they have evolved independently.

21. Limitation of method 3. Organisms which are similar might be found on different continents due to continental drift and be mistakenly classified into different groups or taxa.

22. Quality of written communication: two of [identify method + describe, at least 1 mark + explain limitation, at least 1 mark].

Sources & concepts

Source: DHS Prelim 2023 P3 Q4(a), Section B free-response essay. Stem and the whole key verbatim, including the three-method structure and the quality-of-written-communication rubric. Archetype: evaluate and discuss at essay length, and the classification and phylogeny essay this the papers sets most often. Book 7's essays are outcome-led: this one is LO 4(i) plus LO 4(l) expanded, with LO 4(g)'s biogeography folded in as the third method. Trap: describing three methods and forgetting that half the question is the limitations; the rubric awards a describe mark and an explain-limitation mark for each of two methods, so an essay heavy on description is capped. The scope trap is the taxonomic hierarchy: point 4 asks for three ranks in the correct order and that is the whole of what the ranks are worth, because taxonomy, taxa, genus and kingdom all are not in the learning outcomes. Learn them as vocabulary for reading a question, not as content. LOs: 4(i) throughout, defining biological classification and describing how evolutionary relationship is established. 4(l) in points 13 to 18, the advantages and limits of molecular methods. 4(g) in points 19 to 21, biogeography, and in points 9 to 11, homology against analogy. Concepts fused: (1) morphological comparison as a method; (2) hierarchical nesting; (3) the ranks in order; (4) similar structure inferred to be inherited; (5) subjectivity as a limitation; (6) analogy mistaken for homology; (7) homology missed because the structures look too different; (8) morphology unable to resolve within a clade; (9) sequence alignment and comparison; (10) quantifiability; (11) conserved positions as evidence of ancestry; (12) DNA unavailable from poor fossils; (13) partial-genome sampling as a limitation; (14) biogeographic distribution as a method; (15) continental drift as its limitation. Declared overlaps in this drill, and there are three.** The advantages of molecular methods are stated in Q4(d) as a one-mark reason, argued in Q7(a) as a two-mark explain, and set against their own limitations here at essay length; the three schemes score different things and the essay is capped on description. Multiple sequence alignment appears in Q6(d) as the method you have to explain performing, and in Q7(b) as the phrase the scheme makes compulsory. Reproductive isolation appears in Q1 as the definition's test, in Q2 as the endpoint of speciation, and in Q3 as the barriers themselves; no two of those schemes accept the same answer.
